name: rituals

attributes.attribute: farming god who made waste grow
king wed to the land spirit

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Celtic rites bound a mixed economy, the herd and the wheel both. A farmer drove one's flock between the Beltane fires to guard the beasts. A handful of fruit was offered to the god Crom Dubh at Samhain. The two acts kept the fields in fruit and the herds whole. Still, the yield of a region could swing on a royal tie. The Irish felt that the king was bound to the spirit of that ground. When a king failed in that law, the ground lost its yield. The Welsh had a farming god of their own named Amaethon. Amaethon appears in the poem Kulhwch and Olwen as a man of the field. He could make even the barest ground bloom. No ritual to him was ever set down.

okr.objective: Rituals of the Celtic kept the herd and the field in working shape.
key_results: Beltane fires guarded the driving flock.
Crom Duch got a fruit at Samhain.
The king's wise rule freed the region's yield.
No rite was recorded for Amaethon.
